opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because I think most people focus on the other end of the pipeline: AI solving problems, running experiments faster, predicting structures, crunching data. Defining the problem is the harder and more interesting part.

Right now AI is very good at working inside a well-posed question. If you tell it the objective and the constraints, it can search a huge space far better than we can. But deciding which question is worth asking has always been the deeply human core of science. It comes from taste, from intuition, from noticing that something doesn't quite fit and having the stubbornness to chase it.

Where I see AI changing things is in widening the field of view. A researcher can only read so many papers, only hold so many datasets in mind. AI can surface connections across disciplines, point out anomalies nobody has looked at carefully, or show that two communities are working on the same problem in different languages. So it becomes a kind of collaborator in problem discovery: not deciding what matters, but making the landscape of possible questions much richer and more visible.

There's a risk too. If everyone uses similar models trained on similar literature, we could converge on the same "obvious next questions" and lose the diversity that makes science work. Some of the biggest breakthroughs came from people asking questions that looked unreasonable at the time. So I'd say the ideal is AI expanding our imagination while humans keep responsibility for judgment and taste. Deciding what's worth knowing is still something scientists have to own.

r001.rationale: The candidate says choosing which questions are worth asking depends on human taste and intuition, and that AI should not decide what matters.

r002.rationale: The candidate says AI can work inside a well-posed question and search within its objectives and constraints, but does not state that AI helps refine or structure a problem initially supplied by humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is actually the most interesting question in the whole AI-for-science conversation, because defining the problem is the part of research we've traditionally treated as the most human.

When I was doing the twisted bilayer graphene work, the hard part wasn't running the measurements. The hard part was deciding that this particular angle, this particular system, was worth months of fabrication when most people thought it was a curiosity. That judgment came from a mix of reading the theory, tacit knowledge from the lab, and honestly a bit of stubbornness. Nobody handed us the problem statement.

Right now, AI is very good at the stage after that. Once you have a well-posed question, it can search the literature, propose candidate materials, run simulations, even suggest experimental parameters. That compresses the cycle enormously. But the models are still mostly reflecting back what the field already considers interesting, because that's what they were trained on. They're good at the median problem.

Where I think it gets genuinely new is in connecting things across fields that no single person reads. A lot of good problems sit in the gaps between communities. If a model can notice that an anomaly in one subfield looks like a solved question in another, that is problem definition, in a real sense. I've started seeing early versions of this where the system doesn't give you an answer, it gives you a better question than the one you asked.

So my honest view is that AI won't replace taste anytime soon, but it will change what taste is for. The scientist's job shifts from knowing a lot to knowing what's worth knowing, and being able to tell when the machine's suggested question is actually deep versus just plausible-sounding. That second skill is going to matter a lot more than it used to.

r001.rationale: The response says AI mostly reflects existing ideas about what is interesting, is good at median problems, and will not replace scientific taste anytime soon.

r002.rationale: It says AI can work from a well-posed human question and describes systems that suggest a better question than the one asked.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between solving a scientific problem and deciding which problem is worth solving. AI can help enormously with the first. Once you have a clear objective, it can search for patterns, test possibilities, and help you work through a much larger space of ideas.

But defining the problem requires judgment. What is missing from our understanding? Which assumption should we question? If we answer this question, will it change how we understand the system, or will we simply have one more result?

AI can contribute there, too. It might reveal an unexpected pattern that prompts us to ask a question we wouldn’t otherwise have considered. So I see it as an iterative process: we propose a question, AI helps us explore it, and what we learn changes the question. The scientist’s role is still to judge why that question matters and what evidence would actually answer it.

r001.rationale: The response reserves judgment about a question’s importance for the scientist, but does not clearly state that AI currently lacks the scientific taste to select a research problem independently.

r002.rationale: It describes scientists proposing a question, AI helping explore it, and what they learn changing the question, which communicates AI’s role in refining a human-supplied problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI’s role goes beyond helping us solve a problem once we’ve defined it. It can also help us notice patterns, identify gaps in our understanding, and suggest questions we might otherwise overlook.

But there’s a distinction between generating a question and recognizing that it’s scientifically important. A model might find a correlation that’s very strong statistically, yet doesn’t tell us much about the underlying mechanism. As researchers, we still have to ask: Why does this matter? What would we learn by answering it? And can we design an experiment that distinguishes between competing explanations?

So I see this as an iterative process. We bring some intuition and a broad direction; AI helps us explore the possibilities; then experiments constrain and reshape the question. The exciting possibility is that AI could help us move beyond questions that are simply familiar or convenient to ask, toward questions that reveal something genuinely new.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can suggest questions but researchers must judge why a question matters and what it would teach, conveying that AI cannot independently select a scientifically important problem.

r002.rationale: The response says humans provide intuition and direction and AI explores possibilities, but it does not clearly state that AI helps refine or structure the research problem they initially supplied.
